_about: Hook taxonomy built from essays that admissions offices published themselves (JHU, Connecticut College, Hamilton, Tufts), checked 2026-10-24. Opening of each essay hand-labelled. Essay text is NOT stored — only links, labels and paraphrased "moves".
findings: A third (33%) of admitted essays open on a concrete scene, mid-action. It is the safest strong hook.
Only 14% open reflectively ("Ever since I was little…") — and 2 of the 3 "Why Hopkins" supplements in the sample do. A weak first line is survivable; a vague essay is not.
High-risk/high-reward formats (recipe, file archive, narrator robot, pop quiz) are 11% — they work when the format itself says something about the writer.
Not one published essay opens with an achievement ("I won…", "As president of…"). Achievements live in the activity list; the essay shows the person.
Almost every strong opening has a concrete noun, number or proper name in sentence 1, and a tension or surprise by sentence 2–3.

taxonomy.name: Scene, mid-action
taxonomy.what: Drops the reader into one physical moment — present tense or vivid past — with a sensory detail and a small tension, before any explanation.
taxonomy.why: The reader is inside the writer's head in one sentence; the meaning is earned later instead of announced.
taxonomy.risk: A scene that is pure atmosphere with no tension, or a dramatic moment (injury, game-winning shot) that the rest of the essay never connects to the writer's thinking.
taxonomy.test: Does sentence 1 contain a concrete object, place or action AND a hint that something is about to go wrong or change?

examples.title: In the Belly of the Ship
examples.move: Sweat, a swaying cot and a mosquito net — then the twist that the worst discomfort is shame, not heat.

examples.title: A Splash of Color
examples.move: Taking off a pandemic mask at the mirror before the first unmasked school day; the blush experiment sets up an identity story.

examples.title: Finding My Voice
examples.move: Facing sixty eighth-graders to teach public speaking — then paragraph 2 reveals the writer was born with a speech impediment.

examples.title: Nikeya Tankard ’28
examples.move: Morning hair routine staged as a battle on the bathroom counter — a physical feature becomes an identity essay.

taxonomy.name: Bold or paradoxical claim
taxonomy.what: A short, surprising sentence the reader cannot leave unexplained: a confession, a contradiction, a flat statement of failure.
taxonomy.why: It creates an open question; the essay is the answer. Short sentences read as confident.
taxonomy.risk: Clickbait that the essay never pays off, or a "shocking" claim that is a cliché ("I am a perfectionist").
taxonomy.test: Is it under ~15 words, specific to the writer, and would a stranger ask "wait, what?"

examples.title: A Study in Ambidexterity
examples.move: Claims to have been born with an extra hand, then immediately corrects itself with humour — ambidexterity.

examples.title: Left and Right Don't Exist
examples.move: States a pilot-training lesson as a paradox, then grounds it at 36,000 feet.

examples.title: Clean Closet
examples.move: One task never gets checked off a to-do list — a tiny admission that opens an essay about letting go.

examples.title: Jackson Spallone ’28
examples.move: Four words announcing every plant died; failure first, the hobby lesson after.

taxonomy.name: Line of dialogue
taxonomy.what: Opens on someone speaking — a parent, coach, friend, stranger on the phone.
taxonomy.why: Instant voice, relationship and conflict without exposition.
taxonomy.risk: Generic dialogue ("Wake up!" / "You can do it!") or a famous quote. The line must only make sense in THIS writer's life.
taxonomy.test: Could this line appear in anyone else's essay? If yes, cut it.

examples.title: From Yonkers to Accra
examples.move: A teenager on the phone asking a supplier for leak-proof body bags — an alarming request that turns out to be a public-health project.

examples.title: Bridging Polarity
examples.move: A childhood friend's whispered judgement in San Francisco sets up an essay about respecting opposite views.

examples.title: Shaan Merchant ’19
examples.move: A shouted defence of a long word during a family Bananagrams game — the essay is about loving words.

taxonomy.name: Unconventional format
taxonomy.what: The structure itself is the hook: a recipe, a file archive, a pop quiz, a robot narrator, a poem, an inner "council", a calculation.
taxonomy.why: Shows creativity and control before a single claim is made; memorable in a pile of 50 essays a day.
taxonomy.risk: The highest-variance hook. Fails when the gimmick carries no meaning or makes the essay hard to follow. Needs strong writing.
taxonomy.test: Remove the format — does the content still show who the writer is? Does the format itself say something about them?

examples.title: Tymofii Kolisnyk (Class of 2030)
examples.move: Life told as a folder of digital files a future self opens — war, emigration, math research and climbing, each a file name.

examples.title: Fried Rice in One (Not So) Easy Step
examples.move: Pastes a Google recipe, then declares it wrong — and explains why through family.

examples.title: Beep bop beep bop. I’m Pebble.
examples.move: Narrated by the Lego robot the writer built in 5th grade.

examples.title: Benjamin Frenkel (Class of 2030)
examples.move: An imagined council of inner "officials" debating the writer's day.

taxonomy.name: Idea or concept as a lens
taxonomy.what: Opens with a fact, law, legend or object (entropy, salt, a thousand paper cranes, an Oreo) and turns it into a lens on the writer.
taxonomy.why: Signals intellectual curiosity — strong for STEM and academic-interest essays.
taxonomy.risk: Reads like a textbook or a Wikipedia intro if the writer doesn't appear by sentence 3.
taxonomy.test: Is the writer in the first 2–3 sentences? Is the concept one they actually live with, not decoration?

examples.title: Ordering the Disorderly
examples.move: Second law of thermodynamics, then: "I, unlike the universe…" — a planner-obsessed personality.

examples.title: Just Keep Folding
examples.move: The Japanese legend of a thousand cranes taken as a literal challenge in 8th grade.

taxonomy.name: Question to the reader
taxonomy.what: Opens on a question or riddle the essay answers.
taxonomy.why: Works when the question is strange and specific — the answer IS the writer.
taxonomy.risk: Most question openings are weak ("Have you ever wondered…?", "What is success?"). Only odd, concrete questions earn a place.
taxonomy.test: Would the reader be unable to guess the answer?

examples.title: Anonymous
examples.move: What do you get when you combine a needle, a mainframe, clay and the national budget? — the jobs of the women in the writer's family.

examples.title: On Potatoes
examples.move: The "one food forever" small-talk question answered with mock-seriousness.

taxonomy.name: Precise setting or irony
taxonomy.what: Establishes a world through one exact, often ironic detail: a population figure, a misused stop sign, the "best" month in Vermont being the coldest.
taxonomy.why: Humour and precision prove the writer observes closely.
taxonomy.risk: Can drift into travel-writing about a place rather than the person.
taxonomy.test: Does the detail say something about how the WRITER sees things?

examples.title: The Two Sides of America
examples.move: A Mississippi town of 3,000 whose residents still haven't mastered a five-year-old four-way stop.

examples.title: Taylor Barnes (Class of 2030)
examples.move: First trip to Florida — no beaches, no Disney, just an over-air-conditioned convention ballroom where her troop's proposal is debated.

taxonomy.name: Reflective / summary opening
taxonomy.what: "Ever since I was little…", "For as long as I can remember…", "My lifelong dream…", "Growing up in…".
taxonomy.why: It doesn't — this is the weakest opening. It still appears in 14% of published admitted essays, mostly where the BODY carried the essay (and in "Why us" supplements).
taxonomy.risk: Burns the first 2 sentences on information the reader already assumes. Almost always fixable by deleting sentence 1 and starting at the first concrete moment.
taxonomy.test: Delete the first sentence. If nothing is lost, it was a reflective opening.
